sentences.text: Good, good.
How are you, Andy?
This meeting is being recorded.
I'm good, thank you.
Extremely busy and it's really hot in the uk, weirdly so.
Yeah, that's good.
Good.
Busy or annoying busy?
Well, a bit of both.
Wherever clients are involved, it's always annoying busy, isn't it?
So there is a lot of clients being on board.
Pesky clients.
Right.
Paying the bills.
Yeah, right.
But yeah, we're busy.
It's good busy but just it's combined with heat.
So I'm just kind of, I'm on my last legs at the moment.
Just like ah, things for you.
Likewise.
Yes.
Yeah, things are, you know, there.

I've got a lot of irons in the fire and you know, in the process of sort of shifting some of my time from prospecting and marketing to actually working with clients that are paying me, you know, I've been in outbound mode for, you know, a few months and as, as more clients are coming on board, I've gotta, you know, make sure I carve out time to actually do the work they're paying me for.
Good problem to have, right?
It's a good problem.
Yeah, yeah.
It's that point where it's like you can't really be bothered doing too much of the work yourself.
And are you ready to hire team members to do something?
I don't know that I'm gonna do that.
Like right now it's, you know, the work I'm doing is more, it's consultative and so, you know, it's really me and that's what they want.
I'm not sure I want to get back to having to manage employees.
You know, I've been there and I'm a good coach, I'm a good mentor.
You know, I don't, I don't know, day to day management just, you know, kind of get, get bored by it.
I'm just not looking to get back into that.
I mean contractors I think I would work with.
Well and I've, I've done that and I, you know, I'll definitely probably bring on some more of those but not quite there yet with the clients I've got.
Go ahead.
I'm sorry.
Yeah, go on, go for it.
Sorry, you go.

No, so like I, I mentioned before, I've got two bonafide roll up opportunities where both owners have already spoken to friendly competitors and each has one to two of those that are very interested in, in, you know, the rollup concept.
And so you know, you had sent me an outline of a potential structure for, you know, Deal structure and a fee structure and I just had some follow up questions on that.
So.
Yeah, yeah, sure, I do have them.
And apologies again for.
Yeah, no, no worries.
I've just, I'm trying to like keep, keep them at bay and you know, they, you know, they, they're excited by the concept and so.
And at the same time they've got these other parties that are like, yeah, that sounds cool.
Let's, what's the next step?
And you know, I'm answering the questions as best I can, but you know, if it's possible for us to work together on this, that would, that would be my preference.
So, you know, just wanted to talk through some follow up questions that I had about what you put forward.
Yeah, all right, well, I've got your bullet points here.
Should we go through them?
So.
Yeah, sure, yeah.
From the top.
So the onboarding fee is 30k.
It's actually 25k for, for this process.
But basically 25k pounds and 30k in dollars is my recollection.
But maybe.
I think I might have done.
But actually since gone to market it's slightly different.
But what I gave you was our regular M and A fees which are slightly more.
Okay.
But yeah.
Anyway, that initial fee that we get, that's really just for admin stuff, but obviously you would get a cut of that and that just keeps everybody afloat.
So the, the goal per group would be sort of five to eight.
So it'd be a bit of a stipend to keep everybody sort of lubricated while, while we get the, the deal up and running.
But when you say five to eight, you mean five to eight companies.
Yeah, within each group.
Yeah.
Does it, does it have to be that?
I mean, is, isn't it all to get to it, the certain EBITDA number and if you can get there with as few companies as possible, isn't, isn't that the goal?
So if we can, if we can get larger companies on board.

But the thing is that the, the actual metrics they can, you know, if an agency is doing two and a half or three million EBITDA themselves, the metrics that we can give them, the upside that we can give them isn't quite there.
I mean they could almost get pretty good metrics themselves.
So that, that jump that we give them, you know, sort of doubling the value that really comes for, for agencies that are around a sweet spot.
However, if somebody was happy and just said, look, I don't mind being the cornerstone for this, we're doing three and a half million ebitda.
But if you can find me three other businesses or two other businesses that, that would get us over the sort of 6 million EBITDA mark, then yeah, of course it still works.
It works for everybody.
It just where it's less, less effort really.
So.
Okay, so that would definitely be the ideal.
Got it.
So what was the next, how do you define the carry portion?
So the carry portion is the 20% fee that is the upside that we're providing by putting the deal together.
It doesn't include, that's what I thought.
Yeah, it doesn't include the, the five.
Well, it's actually probably around in reality depending on the size of the business, it's around, it's somewhere between 3 and 5% for the broker fee.
That would be a completely separate team.
It would be.
Well in an ideal world it will always be Capital A that's doing that part of it, but it would be a separate team.
Okay, so the carry is the, is the, the 20% on the, on the arbitrage amount.
Yeah, exactly.

It's, it's just the upside and the way we, we put that together is because we're, we're building the, the Holdco and everything that's there so that actually owns all of the, the contracts and then that there would be a pro rata part of that 80% of that company that the, that the sellers would, would get as part of their deal.
So they feel comfortable owning a piece of the Holdco as well while they're waiting for the deal to get done.
And so in, in that context and you know, I, I, I took a stab at mapping this out to you know, talk to some, to one of the owners of it.
If you've got different companies at different levels of ebitda, you know, let's say you've got one company that's doing 8,800,000 and another's doing 1.8 million.
Calculate the, the carry.
You, you'd have to determine what the initial valuation of each of those companies would be.
Right.
So because the odds are they're not all going to have the same EBITDA or they may not all have the same valuation.

Or do you, do you say hey, we have a fixed formula, you know, within, within you know, EBITDA range of this to this, the pre roll up valuation is going to be, you know, 4x to 6x depending on the numbers and then the post number is what it is.
You know, presumably you're, you know, you're targeting 10x or 8 to 12x or whatever it is.
Yeah, so, so it's, it's 5x.
That's, that's the deal.
The deal is they come in at 5x and we exit at 8 to 12.
So and again this is the difficulty of getting too much variance in that base group.
If somebody comes in and they are doing let's say 2 and a half or, or 3 million EBITDA, they would argue, well we're already 7x so the amount of upside that we can give to them is, is a lot smaller.
Obviously if we can get up to about 7,8 million EBITDA then then definitely we would start to hit the double digits which they wouldn't be getting on their own.
So there would still be benefit to, to become part of the group.
But the argument is weaker.
So.
I see.
So then in order to do that you probably got got to bring together companies that are closer together in an E.
Right.
So you know, if you've got one company that I'm just sort of thinking through the, the process.
So let's say I've got a two companies in mind.
For example, one does let's say a smaller ebitda, but they've got a, A, a great client roster that has not been fully tapped.

But if you bring them into an operation, the, the, you know, the CEO can really go after and bring in a lot more business if they're part of a group that was not just the EBITDA arbitrage, it's, it's the operational.
You know, it got companies like that.
Then I guess the process is the process.
Right.
So just to keep it simple, he gets a 5x value.
You know, I guess it really.
Numbers are all right.
Pretty self contributed values for each company that gets to the fold.
Yeah, so sorry I lost a little bit of you at the end there, but just.
Sorry, I know, I don't.
Either.
But he's coming in at a million dollars in ebitda and that is you know, of the pre roll total then they would get 1/5 of the post roll up total.
Yeah, yeah.
So, so and for us Howard, that that's, that's because of our, our reach.
So what we're trying to do is, is we're marketing to everybody.
We're trying to bring in sort of a narrow band of agencies that are around that 1 million to 2 million EBITDA where we can really leverage the multiple arbitrage.
But obviously there is an opportunistic approach as well that we can take.
In your instance, it's more about who you know in your network that would be willing to join this type of roll up.
So it's a slightly different approach and we're probably, there's a more varied, more variance in the sizes of the agencies that are coming on board.
So I would say with that in mind, we would probably just have to look at it on a case by case business.
But it does get complicated if you start giving everybody their own personal valuation and we've done this before with clients and it just causes no end of arguments, I've got to be honest.
And it's kind of a pain that holds up the whole process, so which is why we, we're just shooting for a, a certain size and bring them in.
That makes sense.
Yeah.
The upside is totally what we're giving them.
They're not able to get it on.
And just out of curiosity, if you value the company at 5x and the exit happens, let's say nine months later.
Right.
So I think you had said figure six months to put the players together and six months to take it to market and close the deal.
Let's say in the interim from when they are evaluated to when they're exited, one company's numbers go up and the others goes down.
Yeah, right.
Because the odds are they're not all going to maintain at an even level.
Do you sort of re reprice the valuation based on trailing 12 months or something like that?
I guess it's probably all spelled out in the.
Well, it's on the day that you close kind of or approaching that day of you're gonna have to close the books, say the week before and everybody gets their valuation at that point.
The buyers will do that anyway.
I mean, nine times out of ten when we're doing a transaction, all of those last minute calculations are happening.
How much cash is in the bank?
Is there burn rate?
How much cash do we need?
This all kind of starts to get worked out in that last minute including, you know, what is their actual ebitda.
So we can work out what the, what the valuation is.
So that will all happen in the lead up to the actual exit.
Yeah.
So it's kind of just live information prior to that.
Okay, makes sense.
Yeah.
And then you asked about the cost for the carry.
So that's most likely going to be all legal fees.
There isn't a huge amount of other costs that we're not, not accounting for.
But obviously if something, if something was to happen, it would just come out of that carry portion, I guess.
But you know, as we're, we're costing it up, but it's unlikely.
But so that's.
Those are external fees, right?
Yeah.
Okay.
Yeah.
All right, that makes sense.
And then do we.
We've got all the different scenarios.
Yeah, that was really the bigger question.
Just, you know, understanding, you know, what support I'd get and, you know, how I can make this work.
And again, my goal is not to, to just refer leads and opportunities to you.

You know, my goal is to, you know, work with you on these and really help build them out and, you know, maybe eventually, you know, become a, you know, a strong collaborator with you on, on future deals.
And I want to be able to understand your process so that I can better sell it to, to the others.
I want to sort of be like, you know, an extension of your, of your team here eventually when we work on these kinds of things together.
So I think in the first scenario was you said where I would bring in one or more of the agencies, but I'm not leading the strategy in, in that environment would I be working with.
With Heather and shaping it?
Because part of it is the people I.
I'm bringing in know me and I think it would be something would be lost if I just completely handed them off to somebody else.
You know, I think in scenario A, I don't think that's.
That's something that you want to be involved.
That's not what you're suggesting is it is more scenario B.
So you would take the lead to go out, source the deals, bring the deals in.
So that would be really replacing Heather's role in that.
So Heather is obviously working on multiple different groups.
You know, we're working.
Heather has one that she's leading in the events space herself, which is more about immersive and experiential events, but she's doing that one.
We have an E commerce and a wellness one, and there's a couple other different things.
So she would be taking the lead in those.
And then the ones where you're.
You're bringing those deals in, you're, you're completely replacing, there wouldn't be really any need for two of you doing the same piece of work.
Okay, so if that's the case, if I'm bringing in the full group and leading the strategy, what type of support would.
Would I be able to count on from.
From you and, and from Capital A?
So Capital A should be providing the full structure for the entire process.
So that would include, you know, building the, the holding company and the complete strategy that goes around that.
I mean, this is a what we call A virtual roll up strategy.
So it's something, right, that we, we specialize in.
And we're able to do that, obviously, because of, we are capital A and because we're doing this day in, day out as an M and A advisory and we have the network to do that.
So part of what we are also providing is, is the deal flow.
So for instance, with Heather, we're not relying on her just calling up all of the people that she knows.
We're providing her with, with the leads continuously, every, every day.
So we're doing all of the outbound, the outbound outreach.

And as those leads come in, they're either we will process them and move them forward before handing them to Heather, or Heather will, will pick them up from Ahmed in particular, who does a lot of the deal flow, and then have those first calls once we've established that it is a good lead.
So we're not expecting you to just get on the phone and go through your Rolodex.
It is a collaborative approach right from the start.
Obviously you're saying you've got two or three leads, but we would.
Are you there still?
Can you hear me?
Yeah, I can.
Sorry, sorry, just so I was just saying.
So, yeah, we're there right from the start, through the entire process of finding the deals as well.
So obviously what we want is to have you sort of front the team as the person who has the expertise in the events space.
But you're not necessarily finding those leads initially.
They'll be coming from us as well.
And then we're providing the entire integration or pre integration process as well.
So we'll be bringing our.
Oh, God.
The connection is really bad today.
Sorry, Howard.
Yeah, connection's quite bad today.
So we're providing the, the pre integration part of that as well and bringing these.
Now.
You're frozen.
I think I'm back.
If you're back, I'm back.
Yeah, Yeah.
I don't know what's going on today with Zoom.
I think it might be my satellite dish.
It's the, it's the trees, potentially.
You there?
Okay.
Yep.
So, yeah, so once, once, obviously we've got the leads and we're starting to build the groups, we, we start to do the pre integration work as well.
So what we want to do is put together the story why it works, dig into each of these companies operationally as well.
You know, see what, what, what, what already might integrate and what doesn't and what's going to need more work.
So we're starting to map that out for the private equity or the buyer, whoever it is, we're mapping all of that out so we've got it all ready to go.
You know, it's a big part of the sales pitch will be, yes, these companies haven't been integrated yet, but we've got the entire map here, so we'll be working on that.
And we've got John Simon, who, I don't know if I mentioned him last time, but he's based up in Denver.
But previously he was chief operations officer for Eisenberg, which is a big LA agency and also very, he's very.
Well, I was going to say well known, but he's got a great network, which is part of what we're leaning into as well.
So, so I mean it's really the, the whole process from start to finish that we're, we'll, we're where they're building the group.
And really the, the main role that you're bringing in is that kind of front, front end conversation to, to bring the potential sellers on board.
Okay.
And so would there be a handoff process with, with John or, or Heather?
If I'm, I guess I'm, I'm not 100% clear on the difference between where I bring in.
In the first scenario where he said bring in some of the agents but not leaving the strategy in this scenario.
B, it sounds like I am leading the strategy.
Yeah.
So that, that strategy, where does John come in?
Okay.
Yeah.
So I mean it's a completely different role.
So the strategy that we're talking about with the, the, that, that piece that Heather does is based around what types of agencies would fit together in a group.
So Heather obviously completely experienced in, in this role.
She's, she's part of a buy and build before and has built, has been, you know, managing director of big firm in New York.
So she's looking for gaps in the agencies that we're bringing on board.
What other businesses do we need to put in there to make this a complete.
Right, so that's what we're relying on you for, strategy.
It's not necessarily anything else beyond that.
However, obviously as the lead going in there initially as well, you're going to create a good relationship with those sellers.
And so you would be on board for the entire process.
It wouldn't be just, here you go, John, you know, I'm on to the next one.
Although there's an element of that it would still be, you know, providing the glue if you like, and the cushion between those agencies and Capital A and the potential buyer as we bring them.
And John's role is much more operational.
He's looking into each of those businesses and going through absolutely everything that they have in there.
What tech stack are they using, what's their processes look like, how do they get business in, you know, the sales process, etc.

He's looking at all of those operational bits and then he's comparing them with all of the others in the group and seeing which of those needs to make changes or how do we map it all out so that the group becomes congruent as we go to market and just getting that story straight.
So it's not the same sort of leadership that you would be offering.
Right.
Okay.

So it's the, the first part that you mentioned that Heather is doing that sort of identifying the right puzzle pieces to bring together combination of companies that fit the right financial profile, owners are interested in selling or they're at that point and you know, do the, do the organizations complement each other and contribute to a, you know, contribute a narrative that can be built.

The second part that you mentioned, John talks about is sort of once you, I'm guessing once you've got the agency pieces together, is sort of crafting an aggregated SIM for the new co that would be then brought to a PE buyer.
Right.
So we've got all these companies.
It's not just like we've got these, this, you know, these five pieces.
But here's the roadmap for how these pieces fit together into a new company.
Once you agree to buy our, our consortium and all the purchase agreements for the individual companies get triggered, here's the game plan for how we're going to integrate them relatively quickly.
And here's how we're going to, you know, integrate the tech stack and we're going to use this company's, you know, CRM and this guy's going to become the cf.
You know, the leadership team is going to be shuffled like this and is that a fair assessment?
You've got it.
Yeah.

So that's the work that we're doing and you know, we've got to understand as well is we are in a market where we have competitors, you know, investment bankers that have no idea how marketing services work or events companies work.
And they're just going out and they're actually doing this themselves and trying to sell them into pe and they are selling them into pe.
And PE are also unaware that a lot of these companies don't actually fit together.
So they're taking a bunch of companies and then Trying to squeeze them all into the same box.
So it is happening, but we're going to be doing a much better job of it.
And so everybody is involved, including the agencies themselves are going to have a much better time being part of this group than, than get getting shoehorned to these Frankenstein.
They get sold on to private equity and then it's just a nightmare for everybody involved.
Nobody can hit their, their earnouts and, you know, it's just not a nice experience.
Right, right.
Agency groups.
Right.
I, I've got to hop onto another call.
Unfortunately, I got back to backs all of this, but hopefully that answers most of the questions that you sent on the, the email.
Yeah, yeah, I know it does.

I, I'm gonna, I'll put together like a rough Excel that just kind of maps out, you know, what these numbers would look like and I'll send it to you just to make sure I'm on the right page in terms of.

I just want to understand like what the 15% that you're offering me would potentially amount to just in, in sync with what the projected workload is because it's probably, as you mentioned, it's probably about a year long time frame and, and in that time frame, you got to keep, keep the cats herded together, you know, make sure that the, the agencies that are signed on are, you know, kept warm so that they don't walk.
I mean, I know that there's probably, you know, terms in the, in the agreement that prevent that, but still, I imagine that it's.
Yeah.
Not unusual that somebody gets cold feet at some point and you know, says, I don't like these people or, you know, it's taken.
So, yeah, I'll run the numbers based on what you told me and send it to you and you let me know if that's right and then, you know, we can go from there.
Does that sound right?
That sounds great.
Yeah.
So have a look at those.
But very roughly, I mean, if you're getting an 8x on 8 million, you would end up with about a million dollars just shy of, of that as your, your piece.
So that's roughly what it would look like.
But yeah, all good.
You run the numbers, let me know what you think that makes sense to you.
Okay, just.
Can I ask you a quick question because this came up with both people.
How much say did the owners get on who else gets brought into the fold?
Yeah, and they always ask this.
All of them ask it, and they want to just build their own roll up, in which case that's fine.
They can 100% do that, but they would be paying to do that in advance.
So it would just, it would cost them a lot more to do it that way.
But what we would, what I would.
Say is cost them more upfront.
Yeah, yeah.
What I'd say is once we, we have one or two key members on board, then yeah, I wouldn't fight that either.
It is part of the process to have that kind of two way street.
What would make more sense for us now?
And we would, you know, we would get that from the experts, but we have to, it's a balancing act of listening to, to them but also having free hands so that we can go out and build the group.
Right.
We want to maintain good relationships with everybody.
We want everybody to stay in the group.
So it is a bit of a backwards and forwards process, but we have to kind of be really clear.
There's an element of that.
However, we need to be able to, to move and build these groups because we do, you know, we've done it many times with our clients and we understand how it works and we, we can't have somebody.
I mean it would work differently if somebody came in with three and a half million.
They'd done 10 acquisitions themselves, but there's sort of one one to two million EBITDA.
They tend to have not had any acquisition experience.
So it's like it.
We do want their advice, we want them to be involved, but also we just need a free hand to be able to bring in members as well.
And that's what your role is really.
Right, right.
To know or to at least have a good idea of what we should be shooting for and what kind of companies do work.
My absolute experience of it is once you show them the businesses that you're talking to or that you want, they actually go, oh yeah, they're perfect.
So although they would like full control, actually they don't mind the choices that we're making.
So.
Yeah, yeah.
And then just last quick question.

I assume that in most PE deals the owners are going to be asked to keep or roll 20, 25, 30% equity into the new company for a potential second buy to the Apple when the PE firm exits, is that that would still be the case in this scenario?
I assume if it's a PE firm that buys, I would say that they would want some equity rollover.
All right, so that's another upside for the owners as well.
Yeah, exactly.
That they can, they can get it.

But, but I mean the big difference is if they went out of 5x which most, most of these businesses will be offered somewhere in that, that region that they wouldn't get any or, or they would get 20 of that upside.
But we're giving them the value, the valuation on that second bite the first time round.
So it will be, it will still be something that's on the table.
Right, but it will be a bigger 20% than what they would have got.
Yeah, yeah.
So it's a pretty big upside.

They get, they get a, you know, a pretty big upside within the first, you know, six to 12 months and then, you know, potentially they're rolling a portion of that into a new entity that a PE firm is going to look to double or triple over the next five years as well.
So it's a, it's a pretty good, good story to tell.
I think if they, if it's done right, I think challenge is, you know, keeping all the pieces together and you know, I mean, you've done this a bunch of times, right, with this, the virtual roll up.
I've done it with clients.
Yeah.
But these are, these ones are the first ones that we're doing with us in charge, where we're running it under our own brand.
Oh, interesting.
All right, let you go.
I appreciate it.
I'll, I'll shoot you some follow up emails and, you know, hopefully we can see we can work together on a couple of these opportunities.
So.
Yeah, good, good catching up with you.
Stay, stay cool and we'll talk soon.
I will.
All right, brilliant.
Have a great day.
Howard, good to see you.

summary.overview: The Business Development and Strategy Discussion meeting between Howard Givner and Andy Day focused on several key topics concerning potential roll-up opportunities and collaboration strategies. Both participants are currently engaged with their clients, with Howard transitioning towards paid client work and expressing a preference for utilizing contractors over managing employees. They discussed two specific roll-up opportunities involving an initial onboarding fee, emphasizing the importance of EBITDA benchmarks for group targets. The valuation process was outlined, indicating that standard valuations typically hover around 5x EBITDA, with exit targets potentially reaching 8-12x. Howard proposed different collaboration scenarios, ranging from a partnership approach where Capital A plays a supportive role in strategy to a more integrated involvement in deal leadership. Integration processes will be managed by John Simon, who will oversee operational alignment across targeted companies. Key action items included Howard creating a financial model to illustrate potential outcomes for review by Andy, reinforcing their collaborative approach to business development.
